title: Anthropic launches Cyber Mission — critical-infrastructure program and free OSS scanner
subtitle: The two-track program pairs frontier Claude models with 11 defense partners for power, water, and transport systems, and offers model-generated vulnerability reports to opted-in open-source maintainers.
author: AESOP AI Engine
body: Anthropic announced the Anthropic Cyber Mission on October 8, a long-term program with two tracks. The Critical Infrastructure Defense Program pairs frontier Claude models and on-site engineers with defenders of power grids, water systems, transportation networks, and government systems. Eleven founding partners sign on — Accenture, Booz Allen, CrowdStrike, Deloitte, Dragos, Hitachi, Insane Cyber, Nozomi Networks, Palo Alto Networks, PwC, and Rockwell Automation. The second track, the OSS Scanner, is a free opt-in service modeled on Google's OSS-Fuzz that scans enrolled open-source projects with Anthropic's most capable models and sends model-generated reports to maintainers without human review. Anthropic claims a true-positive rate above 90%.

Scanning widely used open-source code with frontier models at Anthropic's expense is a direct intervention in the economics of security — maintainers who could not previously afford this get it. The catch is that the reports go out unreviewed, so roughly one in ten could misstate severity or exploitability. For critical infrastructure, pairing frontier models with named cyber-defense partners is a bet that AI will eventually favor defenders over attackers — Anthropic says it expects that shift in about two years, with the near term still uncertain.

The news lands against the Microsoft Digital Defense Report that documented autonomous attack chains, Anthropic's own September disclosure of four misuse incidents involving Claude, and the Pwn2Own Ireland round where researchers deployed AI tools against enterprise infrastructure. Since June, Anthropic has already offered Claude and support to more than half of US states and some large public infrastructure operators under the earlier Project Glasswing. The industry is converging on the same question — whether defenders can scale their advantages faster than attackers scale theirs.

If you contribute to or depend on an open-source project, this program is a chance to see how AI-generated vulnerability reports look in practice. Treat the reports as leads, not verdicts — reproduce every bug yourself before patching, because an unreviewed model finding can be wrong about severity, exploitability, or both. The skill worth building now is triage, not trust, and it is the same skill that will separate useful AI-assisted security engineers from the ones who paper over the stack.
